15.layer4: Both Sunni and Shia exegetes interpret this verse as affirming divine sovereignty and the perfection of Allah's judgments. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah does not fear anyone seeking revenge for those He destroyed or holding Him accountable for His decisions, because He is the ultimate authority answerable to none. Al-Razi discusses the verse as negating any limitation or fear from Allah, establishing His absolute power and independence. Tabrisi similarly emphasizes that Allah's destruction of the Thamud was entirely just, and no consequence of that action could cause Him any concern because His power and authority are absolute. Both traditions connect this verse to numerous others affirming that Allah is questioned about nothing He does while all others are questioned about their deeds. Classical scholars across both schools discussed the verse as establishing the proper relationship between Creator and creation - absolute authority on one side, complete accountability on the other. Both Sunni and Shia interpretation emphasize that this verse should inspire both fear of divine judgment and trust in divine justice. The verse concludes Surah Ash-Shams by affirming that ultimate power, knowledge, and justice rest with Allah alone.
15.layer4_urdu: سنی اور شیعہ دونوں مفسرین اس آیت کو الٰہی حاکمیت اور اللہ کے فیصلوں کی کمال کی تصدیق کے طور پر سمجھتے ہیں۔ ابن کثیر وضاحت کرتے ہیں کہ اللہ کسی سے نہیں ڈرتا جو ان کا انتقام لے جنھیں اس نے تباہ کیا یا اس کے فیصلوں کے بارے میں اسے جوابدہ ٹھہرائے، کیونکہ وہ کسی کے سامنے جوابدہ نہ ہونے والی حتمی اتھارٹی ہے۔ الرازی آیت پر بحث کرتے ہوئے اللہ پر کسی محدودیت یا خوف کی نفی کرتے ہیں اور اس کی مطلق طاقت اور آزادی کو قائم کرتے ہیں۔ طبرسی نے بھی اسی طرح زور دیا کہ اللہ کا ثمود کو تباہ کرنا مکمل طور پر عادلانہ تھا اور اس عمل کا کوئی نتیجہ اسے کوئی فکر نہیں پہنچا سکتا کیونکہ اس کی طاقت اور اختیار مطلق ہے۔ دونوں روایات متعدد دیگر آیات سے ربط قائم کرتی ہیں جو تصدیق کرتی ہیں کہ اللہ سے اس کے کسی کام کے بارے میں سوال نہیں کیا جا سکتا جبکہ سب دوسرے اپنے اعمال کے بارے میں جوابدہ ہیں۔ دونوں مکاتبِ فکر کے کلاسیکی علماء نے اس آیت کو خالق اور مخلوق کے درمیان صحیح تعلق قائم کرنے کے طور پر بیان کیا۔ سنی اور شیعہ دونوں تفاسیر اس بات پر زور دیتی ہیں کہ یہ آیت الٰہی فیصلے کا خوف اور الٰہی عدل پر اعتماد دونوں کو اکسانی چاہیے۔ سورۃ الشمس کا اختتام تصدیق کرتا ہے کہ حتمی طاقت، علم اور انصاف صرف اللہ کے پاس ہے۔
15.layer4_ar: يتفق المفسرون السنة والشيعة على أن هذه الآية تُثبت السيادة الإلهية وكمال أحكامه. ويُبيِّن ابن كثير أن الله لا يخشى أحداً يسعى للثأر ممن أهلكهم أو يُحاسبه على قراراته لأنه السلطة القصوى التي لا تُساءل. ويتناول الرازي الآية بوصفها نفياً لكل قيد وخوف عن الله، مُؤسِّسةً قدرته المطلقة وغناه التام. ويُؤكد الطبرسي بالمثل أن إهلاك الله لثمود كان بالغ العدل ولا يترتب على ذلك الفعل أي تبعة يمكن أن تُشغل باله سبحانه لأن قدرته وسلطانه مطلقان لا حدود لهما. ويربط التراثان الآية بكثير من الآيات الأخرى المُقررة أن الله لا يُسأل عما يفعل وجميع الخلق مسؤولون عما يفعلون. وقد ناقش علماء كلا المذهبين الآية بوصفها مُؤسِّسةً العلاقة الصحيحة بين الخالق والمخلوق - سلطان مطلق في جانب ومساءلة تامة في الجانب الآخر. ويُبرز التفسيران السني والشيعي معاً أن هذه الآية ينبغي أن تُلهم في الوقت ذاته خشية الحكم الإلهي والثقة بعدله وحكمته. وتختتم هذه الآية سورة الشمس بتقرير أن القدرة الحقة والعلم المحيط والعدل الكامل لله وحده لا شريك له.
15.layer1: The final verse of Surah Ash-Shams, verse 15, closes with an awe-inspiring declaration: 'And He does not fear the consequences thereof.' This statement refers to Allah's act of destroying Thamud. Unlike a human ruler, king, or general who destroys his enemies but must consider the political repercussions, the reaction of other powers, or the risk of retaliation, Allah has absolutely no fear of any consequence. His sovereignty is total, His power is unrivaled, and His justice is supreme. No force in creation can threaten, question, or avenge itself against Him. This final verse serves multiple functions within the surah. First, it underscores the absolute sovereignty of Allah, a theme that resonates powerfully with the Meccan audience who were used to seeing powerful tribal leaders fear consequences before acting. Second, it serves as an implicit warning to those who persecute the Prophet Muhammad and the early Muslim community: just as the powerful Thamud were annihilated without Allah fearing any reprisal, so too will the Quraysh find no refuge from divine justice if they persist in their transgression. Third, it provides spiritual reassurance to the oppressed believers that the justice of Allah, when it comes, is comprehensive and complete. The verse ends the surah on a note of absolute divine authority that brings the entire structure of the surah full circle. The oaths that opened the surah pointed to divine power embedded in creation; this final verse asserts that divine power faces no limitation and no accountability to any created being.
15.layer2: Ibn Kathir records in his tafsir that Ibn Abbas, the great companion and Quran exegete, explained this verse by saying: 'Allah does not fear any consequences from anyone.' The same explanation was given by Mujahid, al-Hasan al-Basri, Bakr ibn Abdullah al-Muzani, and several other leading scholars of the tabi'in generation. Al-Tabari in Jami al-Bayan records all these narrations through their complete chains of transmission and notes that this is the unanimous understanding of the Salaf for this verse. The phrase wa-la yakhaf uqbaha can be read in two grammatical interpretations: first, that the subject is Allah and He does not fear any consequence from His punishment of Thamud; second, that the subject refers to the punishment itself, meaning it does not fear or spare anything in its path. Classical scholars overwhelmingly preferred the first reading, which is the one transmitted from Ibn Abbas and the consensus of the early exegetes. Al-Qurtubi adds an important theological dimension, noting that this verse affirms the divine attribute of absolute independence, Al-Ghina, combined with absolute power. Unlike human sovereigns whose acts of punishment are constrained by fear of consequences, Allah's justice is unconstrained by any external consideration. This is related to the theological discussion of divine simplicity and sovereignty in Sunni kalam. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb develops this further by connecting the verse to the divine names Al-Qawi (the Strong) and Al-Aziz (the Mighty), arguing that the absence of fear in Allah's act is not indifference but the expression of perfect power.
15.layer3: Sayyid Qutb concludes his commentary on Surah Ash-Shams in Fi Zilal al-Quran with a meditation on this final verse that is among his most theologically rich passages. He writes that the surah began by presenting the universe as a vast theatre of divine signs, from the cosmic grandeur of the sun and moon down to the intimate drama of the human soul, and it ends with this declaration of absolute divine sovereignty that removes any final doubt about the nature of the power behind those signs. Qutb observes that for the first Muslims in Mecca, this verse was not merely theological information but direct spiritual sustenance. They were a persecuted minority facing a powerful tribal society, and the reassurance that the God on whose side they stood fears no consequence from any worldly power was transformative for their resolve. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir relates this verse to the broader Quranic theme of divine transcendence over human political structures. Every human form of governance operates under constraint: fear of rebellion, fear of stronger powers, fear of historical judgment. Allah alone is free from all such constraints, and His justice is therefore the only truly reliable justice. Ibn Uthaymeen reflected that this verse is also a reminder to believers not to delay righteous action out of fear of human consequences, for the believer who truly internalizes this verse understands that only Allah's judgment ultimately matters. The surah thus ends as it began, with an affirmation of divine majesty that invites the human soul to align itself with the truth rather than with the fleeting powers of this world.
